Aspiration Action Achievement
Set goals and targets to drive your everyday experience, and have dreams to follow in the long term.
Work to reach your goals and make your dreams become reality. It may be hard, but it will be worth it.
Gain qualifications and skills and value everything you do that takes you one step closer to your dream.
“The staff team works together exceptionally well, with respect, collaboration and commitment to the pupils.”
School
Shaftesbury School is a vibrant learning environment, providing students with the opportunity to prosper both academically and personally. Our aim is to see every student succeed in achieving their goals and being the best they can be.
Sixth Form
We are immensely proud of our Sixth Form and the outstanding level of education and academic rigour provided to our students. This is demonstrated by the consistent improvement in student outcomes that we are delighted to witness each year.
Welcome to Shaftesbury School
As the Headteacher I am both delighted and immensely proud to lead the school as we strive for excellence.
Each child arrives as an individual, and the school’s heart and soul goes into developing that individuality together with a sense of social and moral responsibility and a love of learning, encouraging children to live life in all its fullness.

We would like to introduce you to the Dorset based young carers charity MYTIME. We are now working in partnership with MYTIME Young Carers to support and celebrate young carers within our school community.
Who are Young Carers?
A young carer is a child, under the age of 18, who spends time looking after or helping to look after a family member. Most young carers look after a parent or a sibling but can be caring for more than one person, for example, a parent and a sibling.
• Someone living with a mental health condition
• Someone misusing substances such as alcohol or drugs
The range of care, and time spent caring, can vary, but every young carer carefully balances their schoolwork and social life. Without support, caring responsibilities can have a big impact on a child’s life.
No two young carers’ needs are the same, which is why MYTIME offer a range of programs, created to meet the needs of young carers, designed, and driven by young carers themselves.
Who are MYTIME Young Carers?
MYTIME Young Carers currently work in 200 schools across Dorset and BCP. They offer a range of programs which young carers can access. Young carers can access online youth groups, activity days and other fun opportunities via the Making Memories program.
I think my child is a young carer, what next??
• Speak to school: either email the office or speak to your child’s teacher
• Register with MYTIME Young Carers: If you would like your child to access the opportunities offered by MYTIME Young Carers then please follow this link and fill in our online form:
MYTIME Programme Registration
• Once your child is registered with MYTIME you will receive regular updates. Young Carers can become involved in MYTIME’s fun Online Zoom Youth Group, where they get to take part in different activities and meet other young carers (all from the comfort of your own home!)
• Your child will also be able to attend MYTIME’s amazing Making Memories events. Most of these happen in the school holidays and range from a trip into the woods at Adventure Pirates to a day of sailing or paddleboarding. MYTIME also run art and craft events, and even host their very own Young Carer’s Festival in August.
• To find out more, or if you have any further questions regarding the opportunities MYTIME offer please contact MYTIME on: enquiries@mytimeyoungcarers.org
Young Carer Champion: Mrs Burfitt

Curriculum Overview
Modern Foreign Languages
At Shaftesbury School, we aim for Modern Foreign Languages (MFL) to provide a valuable educational, social and cultural experience for pupils; preparing them to be global citizens in the wider world.
As a Languages Department we believe in the provision of a broad and balanced curriculum. The aim of the curriculum is to provide access to modern language learners of all abilities. Modern Foreign Languages are offered at KS3, KS4 and KS5 within the normal school day. Languages are compulsory at KS3 and 2/3 of our students take it at KS4. KS5 is optional. The department is also committed to the enrichment of other aspects of the school curriculum through MFL and International dimension initiatives.
Key Stage Three
Key Stage 4
Students who study a language at GCSE study for 6 hours per fortnight. They have reserved time in ICT suites and for I pad usage. They will also work with our 6th Form Foreign Language Interns.
The Spanish GCSE group will have the option to attend our very popular and successful residential exchange with our link school in Jaen. In addition we are working hard to establish a link with a French school so that the French GCSE students can also benefit from taking part on a residential exchange.
Key Stage 5
Shaftesbury students can study French or Spanish at AS and A2 Level. They will be supported to plan and undertake foreign exchange visits, will use a variety of multi-media to support their work. A Level students of French and Spanish are also given the opportunity to work as language interns themselves. They usually support KS4 and KS5 classes.
We also enter students in Sixth Form examination for their mother tongue, and Shaftesbury School students have gained qualifications in Russian, Chinese, Arabic, Polish, Italian, Portuguese and German.

Curriculum Overview: Drama
“Like all the arts, Drama is a learning experience which supports the intellectual and emotional development of young people. “
Drama Curriculum Intent
Like all the arts, Drama is a learning experience which supports the intellectual and emotional development of young people. Our intent is to develop students who are open minded, able to accept constructive criticism and be flexible in their approach. Through drama a special kind of learning takes place which is not always available in other areas of the curriculum. Through active involvement in imagined roles and situations, students engage in direct experiences, experiences which challenges their thinking, makes demands on their language and helps them to work creatively together. We will help students to grasp concepts, explore complex issues and solve problems, whether this be individually or working effectively as part of a group – we consider this an essential life skill and is something we strive to instil in all our students. All students will have an inspiring experience of Drama and Theatre Studies developing both a practical and theoretical appreciation for the subject and world around them as their knowledge and understanding widens.
We believe that Drama should allow all students to express themselves in a safe and supportive environment, as they understand and appreciate the benefits of team work, communication and creativity. In Drama students will learn through many different methods, including scriptwriting, improvising, devising their own material and interpreting scripts. Furthermore, the chosen play texts at KS3, KS4 and KS5 allow all students to experience, analyse and evaluate a wide range of social, cultural and historical aspects developing a deeper knowledge, appreciation and understanding of others and their cultures. Students will engage with our curriculum meaningfully through as much practical work as possible, whilst simultaneously embedding theory into our teaching model. We create an atmosphere where students work with a high level of independence, inventiveness and a willingness to take risks to create articulate, considerate and creative students enhancing skills for life, with and beyond, Shaftesbury School.
Implementation
Our curriculum has been structured to ensure students’ progress from KS3 up to KS5 and beyond. We aim to instil a love of learning through our subject and provide skills and knowledge that are useful in all areas of life inside and outside of the school. All students at Key Stage 3 have two drama lessons every fortnight and this time increases to 6 lessons at GCSE and 8 at A-Level.
In KS3 drama lessons consist of the basic skills of devising, performing and responding to performance. Students will focus on developing and improving their physical and vocal skills and will experiment with a range of drama techniques, conventions, genres and styles. As students move up Key Stage 3 the content of lessons will vary and allow students to not only explore plays, but also devise and write their own material allowing them to create their own content and explore various themes and issues. Students will apply their practical skills within rehearsals and performances and analyse and evaluate their own work and work of others. Students will develop an understanding of how plays are taken from the page to stage, both through practical and theoretical application. They will learn how to write about their own skills, and those of others, demonstrating an understanding of their effect and impact, whilst simultaneously developing subject specific language. The curriculum is varied, challenging and ensures that a range of skills are developed, whilst students are nurtured to become creative, confident and independent learners.
In Key Stage 4 students follow the AQA GCSE course; they will learn to develop their performance skills, have the ability to analyse and evaluate the work of live theatre makers, create devised drama, interpret and perform plays and develop their knowledge and understanding of stage design aspects, including lighting, sound, costume and set design. Students will work both practically and theoretically as they develop their understanding of drama and the theatre and will be encouraged to articulate and express their ideas, views and opinions about a wide range of topics and issues clearly, confidently and respectfully. Students will gain the confidence to pursue their own ideas and reflect and refine their efforts. Skills learnt within Key Stage 3 will continue to develop and improve and the importance of written work will be a focus of the course. Students will have access to a wide range of theoretical materials to support the written element of the GCSE which will allow them to develop their vocabulary in preparation for the Component 1 exam and NEA essays in Component 2. Regular written responses will allow students to develop their language and analysis and evaluative skills and marking and feedback on this work will be pivotal in supporting students – challenging, inspiring and developing their skills even further.
Disadvantaged students will be positively supported through directed questioning and 1:1 assistance within the classroom. We aim to support our students through timely and organised intervention and we provide a range of opportunities for students to catch up on and extend their learning such as after school sessions, sessions during lunch and online provision.
Without doubt, students of Drama emerge with a toolkit of transferable skills, applicable both in further studies, the workplace and society as a whole.
‘There is a balance in all good teaching between formal instruction of content and skills, and giving young people the freedom to inquire, question, experiment, and express their own thoughts and ideas. In creative and cultural education, this balance is essential. Creative learning requires creative teaching.’
Creative and Cultural Education; All Our Futures: A Summary, NCA 2000
Impact
By the end of Key Stage 3 students will have developed a foundation for the study of GCSE Drama at KS4 and will understand the options available for further study. They will be able to recognise and use various drama techniques with confidence and creativity. Students will be able to analyse and interpret scripts as well as create original devised material. In addition, students will be able to play a wide variety of clearly defined characters and demonstrate their knowledge and understanding of a number of different skills, techniques, genres and styles of performance. Students will be able to write more confidently about their dramatic intentions and performance skills, whilst also evaluating their own and others work. Students will be able to express their opinions with growing confidence and work productively and positively, both individually and in groups, further enhancing valuable life skills and broadening horizons.
By the end of Key Stage 4 students will be well rounded performers with a detailed knowledge of the processes of creating live theatre; they will have a thorough understanding of how meaning is communicated, through both performance skills and design aspects. Students will feel confident analysing and evaluating their own work and that of others and will be able to use theatre terminology effectively. They will have an appreciation of the cultural, social and historical aspects of the plays studied and will be able to apply this knowledge and understanding to a range of questions and disciplines varying from costume design, to directing and performing. Students will have explored a variety of play texts and learnt how to thoroughly analyse and evaluate the playwright’s intentions, considering the impact of symbolism and thematic meanings, whilst developing an insightful understanding of characters, plots, relationships and creation of mood and atmosphere. Students will have also devised their own performances based on a stimulus and worked collaboratively, to write, direct and perform in their own piece. They will understand the role of Drama in society and the range of careers in different areas and will be informed and prepared regarding further study of the subject at KS5. Students will have developed a love of reading and appreciation of the Arts, encouraging open mindedness, and to be the best that they can be.
‘I regard the theatre as the greatest of all art forms, the most immediate way in which a human being can share with another the sense of what it is to be a human being’

“Music is an art form that we all have contact with as part of our daily lives and is a valuable outlet for expression. The studying of music allows students to learn about team work, problem solving through practice and improvement, and gain an understanding about the elements of history and other cultures that surround the music they are learning about.”
Music Curriculum Intent 2023 – 2024
Music is an art form that we all have contact with as part of our daily lives and is a valuable outlet for expression. The studying of music allows students to learn about team work, problem solving through practice and improvement, and gain an understanding about the elements of history and other cultures that surround the music they are learning about. Music is both a rewarding and challenging discipline that will allow students to build perseverance, communication skills, motor skills (through the playing of instruments), computing skills, confidence, and creativity. Music can lead to many opportunities and different career pathways outside of the main performance and composition ideals. These include; Sound Production, Music Reviewers, Music Therapists, Arts Management, tour managers and Event organisers.
The overarching concepts for Music at Shaftesbury School are:
As a subject it is separated into three disciplines: Performance, Composing, and Listening & Appraising. At KS3 the three elements are taught holistically to allow students to build upon these skills in an integrated way. The curriculum allows for a wide range of interest and provides experiences with a variety of specialist equipment. We have a specialist music technology room equipped with Macs for students to use, a separate recording studio and live room, and a practical room with keyboards and a variety of other instruments available for the students’ use. Students will gain skills in all three disciplines with termly performances and evaluation-based assessments on their current topic of learning, alongside appraisal and listening assessments. By the end of their time in KS3 they will be able to play and perform on at least one instrument and understand how to read music written for those instruments. This will mean that they can carry forwards these skills into later life if they wish. Each topic learned is linked to the cultural and historical context allowing them a rich knowledge of different areas. Through performance and articulating the meaning behind music, students will gain experience of key life skills such as public speaking, working with others, and cognitive analysis and understand which in turn will build on their cultural capital and knowledge.
Literacy Implementation
The school wide focus on literacy can be found in;
World Music 1: Drumming
Introduction to basic elements of musicality & performing together as an ensemble. Students will start to aurally recognise different musical patterns and textures, and be able to create their own. They will be introduced to the context of music in a different culture. H/A students can lead their groups and act as the master drummer.
Music building Bricks (rhythms)
Students recap skills from unit 3 focusing on rhythmic notation and piano skills. They build on this knowledge by learning about time signatures and rhythmic devices such as ostinatos and syncopation. They will also increase the complexity of their rhythmic notation knowledge by writing their own and practising rhythmic dictation. H/A students will be able to use more complex rhythms and play contrasting rhythms in the right/left hand.
World Music 2: Samba
Students will learn about the cultural context of Samba and its origins. They will build on their previous work on rhythms and drumming patterns by working together as a group to create Samba pieces. They will increase the complexity of their playing by including more challenging rhythmic concepts such as playing cross rhythms and regular syncopations. They will also become more familiar recognising those features when notates.
Continuing to build on musicality and ensemble skills through group singing, and incorporating elements of pitch and harmony into the learning. Students will also practice how to hold a musical line against other parts. There will be links with science and PE by looking into how to correctly warm up our bodies, as well as learning how music and singing specifically can impact our health and brains.
Students build on previous keyboard units with increasing complexity involving hand placement variations and increasing use of left hand. They will also recap pitch notation and build on this by looking at the bass clef, and the use of accidentals and how to play sharps/flats. H/A students (or students who already play piano will bring in a piece they are working on and create a practice diary and schedule to showcase their development.
Music Theatre (performance)
Students build on their instrumental skills by learning to read chord charts for both guitar and keys, as well as drum notation, as well as learning to basic patterns on these instruments. They will apply their knowledge about chord formation from the previous unit to realise the patterns in their pieces. Students will build on ensemble and performance skills and perform their outcomes to the class at the end of the unit.
Piano skills 1- The theory behind music (keyboard skills)
Introduction to notation and keyboard skills. Working towards building and improving dexterity on Keyboards, and recognising rhythmic and pitch notation. This will allow students to take on more challenging performance tasks in future modules. H/A students (or students who already play piano will bring in a piece they are working on and create a practice diary and schedule to showcase their development.
Minimalism (composition)
Students will look at different compositional devices that can be used as a form of rhythmic and melodic development. They will apply this through composing their own piece based on this genre. They will look at similarities to Gamelan and the context behind gamelan (world music).
Classical Variations (composition)
Building on previous units looking at melodic and rhythmic development, whilst linking it with harmony skills that have been learnt in previous units. Students will create their own set of variations on a theme combining all of the skills they have built in composition in previous units. They will also work on aural recognition through listening exercises.
Introduction to the orchestra
Students will learn about the different instruments and their families. They will also learn about how to select sonorities for certain pieces and write idiomatically for an instrument. They will also be introduced music tech software and start to compose their own pieces.
Introduction to key elements of Jazz and blues music. They will learn about how to improvise on a set scale and create their own blues pieces. They will build their independence and ensemble skills by working in groups to create their pieces. They will learn about the cultural and historical impact and context of the blues creating links with history, and English through the writing of lyrics.
Rock and Pop (theory and history)
Recapping and linking to previous topics looking at chords, and Jazz and Blues, students will learn about common chord progressions and how they are used in different songs. They will learn the musical elements of popular music. They will also learn about how pop music can be used as a tool to reflect political and cultural issues of the time they are written. They will discover how composers write idiomatically for voice and apply their previous knowledge of melodic and rhythmic development to writing a song. They will also learn about the theory behind chords and how diminished/augmented/major/minor and how these sounds can alter the mood of a piece. H/A students will apply this to their compositions.
Music and Space (sonorities and performance)
Students will build on their knowledge of instruments and sonorities by looking at how composers create music for a certain theme (space). They will learn about the context of different pieces and link them with historical events. They will learn further about the elements of music and how they are used in pieces. They will further build on their ensemble skills from unit 1 & 2 by learning pieces with independent lines, this time on different instruments (keyboards, guitars, drums & instruments that students play).
Film Music (history, theory and performance)
Building on their previous knowledge of sonorities and how the different elements of music can link to certain themes, students will discover how composers write music to accompany action on screen. They will build on their performance skills by learning to play famous leitmotifs, as well as analyse how those leitmotifs link musically to the character/idea they’re portraying. They will learn the history of film music, and how it has developed over time and its links to classical composers.
Rock and Pop (performance)
Students will build on ensemble and instrumental skills with an increase in complexity from previous units to create a performance of a pop song. They will be able to plan a rehearsal schedule, and evaluate their practices and performances.
Music and Space 2 (Music Technology)
Continuing to build on music technology skills from unit three, students will explore how to use effects and automations to increase the musicality of a composition. They will also apply the knowledge of musical elements discovered in the previous term to create their own composition.
Film Music (Composition)
Students will apply the knowledge from the previous unit by creating their own film music compositions to accompany a clip. They will also build on their music tech skills from previous units incorporating the use of effects, automations, samples and manipulation of MIDI.
World Music 3 (Indian Music)
Students will be introduced to music from different areas of the globe. They will learn about the context and meaning behind the music and how the practice differs to our own through listening, composing, and performing.
Students rotate topics every half term. These topics consist of 6-8 lessons per rotation based on a 40 week program.
The National Curriculum for music aims to ensure that all pupils:• Perform, listen to, review and evaluate music.• Be taught to sing, create and compose music.• Understand and explore how music is created, produced and communicated.
We teach the OCR Music GCSE. Through this, students learn about 4 key areas of study; The concerto through time, Film and Video Game music, World music, and Pop Music. This creates a broad depth of knowledge of many different genres, as well as teaching the historical and cultural context around each area. We teach these topics by combining theoretical knowledge and appraisal (listening and evaluating) skills with practical application of these skills through compositions or performances in each of these genres. As part of the course, they have two examined compositions, one of which is ‘free’ and they choose their style and genre, and the other is responding to a set brief provided by the exam board. Additionally, they have two performance, one ensemble and one solo which build on the performance practiced gained in KS3.
Extra-Curricular: We currently have a number of extra-curricular sessions available. Please see these under Extra Curricular.
Instrumental Lessons
We also offer individual instrumental/vocal lessons. These take place in school during the school day. We currently offer Voice, Piano, Guitar, Drums, Violin, Flute, Oboe.
To request instrumental lessons, please complete this FORM.
Your details will be passed on to the relevant teacher who will be in touch to organise times and payments. If your child wishes to receive instrumental lessons but you are concerned about funding please contact Abigail.fiddik@shaftesburyschool.co.uk.

pageCache.pageTitle: Pastoral Care and House System - Shaftesbury School
pageCache.text:
Shaftesbury School maintains an excellent reputation for pastoral care. We understand the importance of a system that students can access during these exciting, yet challenging times at school and one that contributes in creating a safe and enjoyable place for students to thrive. We place great importance on developing resilience and self-esteem in all students, whilst at the same time promoting an environment where all students feel they belong, are valued and are listened to. The pastoral teams work together with parents, staff, students and external agencies to allow our young people to ‘be the best they can be’.
Pastoral Teams in Shaftesbury School
Our Pastoral Teams at Key Stage 3, 4 and 5 are each led by a Year Leader, with a member of the Senior Team or Head of Sixth Form overseeing this. The teams have responsibility for the academic progress, behaviour and attendance of each student, whilst supporting wellbeing and providing pastoral care. They lead a dedicated and committed team of tutors who see their tutor groups each morning 08.30-8.40 and then again at 13.35-14.00. The tutor is the day-to-day contact for all students and stand as the primary link between parents and school.
Key Stage 3 & 4 Year Teams
Students are arranged in year tutor groups and still have an allocation to a house.
Mrs S. Savage – (Static) Head of Year 7 and leads Melbury House – Senior Leader link is Mr M. Dean – Assistant Headteacher

pageCache.pageTitle: Behaviour at Shaftesbury School - Shaftesbury School
pageCache.text:
Behaviour at Shaftesbury School is based upon the principle that all members of the school should be treated and treat others fairly, honestly, and with respect and in line with our vision for education, reflecting that of the Church of England, asking for everyone ‘to be the best they can be’. Inclusive in our vision is the common good of the whole community and its environment. We welcome diversity, respect freedom of religion and belief and encourage all to contribute to our community.
Promoting and rewarding good behaviour
We are committed to the modelling and teaching of good behaviour. Staff recognise that lesson content, classroom management, organisation and teaching and learning strategies are all contributory factors to student behaviour. Staff will use various rewards to track and celebrate good behaviour.
Students are encouraged to reach the highest standards both in terms of their work and personal development. A range of measures are used to reward students’ achievements and progress.
Attendance certificates;
Attendance reward breakfasts;
Shaftesbury School expectations
On a daily basis, student are expected to follow basic expectations to help them ‘be the best they can be’.
Arrive on time
Respect others
Expect to learn
Be smart in their appearance
Be prepared for the lesson
Electronic devices turned off and in bags
Challenge themselves and aim high
Take responsibility for their behaviour
Aspire. Action. Achieve
Conduct Cards
We place great importance on students being able to experience a safe and respectful atmosphere here at Shaftesbury School. We also believe in the importance of students being given the opportunity to self-regulate their own behaviour. At times, our young people may need support with this. All students carry two ‘Conduct Cards’ around with them for a term. One to reward positive, aspirational behaviour around school and one to tackle negative behaviour around school. Each time they are seen to be demonstrating either conduct, they obtain a signature on their corresponding card. The aim with these cards is to provide the students with three chances to ‘get it right’ with a visual representation of their reward/offence explained and shared with parents.

pageCache.text:
Dorset Mental Health Support Team in Schools
Mental Health Support Teams (MHST) in schools are part of a joint national initiative between the Department of Education and NHS England to improve access to psychological therapies (IAPT) for children and young people presenting with emerging low mood and mild to moderate anxiety within an educational environment.The 3 core functions of the teams are:
Education Mental Health Practitioners (EMHP’s) work as part of the MHST in Schools delivering 1:1 work with young people and/or their families. EMHP’s also deliver workshops in schools to whole classes and run groups for young people and groups for parents/carers. EMHP’s are the people your children are most likely to see in school.
Please speak to your child’s Tutor or Head of Year or a member of the School Leadership Team if you feel you would benefit from support from the MHST.For further information on the MHST in Schools, please visit:
Dorset Mind
www.DorsetMind.co.uk
Dorset Mind is one of over 100 Local Minds that provide essential mental health servicesin local communities across England and Wales.
Active Monitoring
Active Monitoring gives people aged 11-18, through a programme of 1-2-1 guided self-help sessions, the opportunity to explore their feelings and emotions with a friendly trained practitioner.
Referrals can be made via GPs and healthcare professionals. This service is currently run out of certain GP surgeries. Please see our website for more information. Young People Active Monitoring – Dorset Mind
young people active monitoring – dorset mind
Kooth.com – online support for young people
Kooth offers young people the opportunity to have a text-based conversation with a qualified counsellor. Counsellors are available from 12 noon to 10pm on weekdays and 6pm to 10 pm at weekends, every day of the year on a drop-in basis. Young people can access regular booked online counselling sessions as needed. Outside counselling hours, young people can message our team and get support by the next day.
There is no threshold for students to access support through Kooth.
When students register with Kooth they will have support available to them now and in the future. Support can be gained not only through counselling but articles, forums and discussion boards. All content is age appropriate, clinically approved and fully moderated.
To find out more visit www.Kooth.com where young people can register and others can find out more about the service.
You can also view a short video about the service
Kooth provides online, confidential, mental health and well-being support to young people aged 11–18 years in Dorset via any internet accessible device. Kooth provides an opportunity to interact in a supportive way with other young people as well as receive support from a qualified counsellor.
Place2Be
Place2Be is a children’s mental health charity with over 25 years’ experience working with pupils, families and staff in UK schools. We provide mental health support in schools through one-to-one and group counselling using tried and tested methods backed by research.

Shaftesbury School is committed to tackling and preventing homophobic, biphobic and transphobic bullying.
The Public Sector Equality Duty requires all schools to eliminate discrimination, advance equality of opportunity, and foster good relations between people.
The Equality Act 2010 lists ‘gender reassignment’ and ‘sexual orientation’ as protected characteristics. As a school we have a duty to make sure that our students are not discriminated against because they are LGBTQ+.
As a Church of England school, we know that many people of faith are also LGBTQ+, and do not feel that the two are in opposition. It’s vital for us as a faith and church school that we ensure LGBTQ+ people of faith don’t face extra stigma for being who they are.
If you have any questions or concerns, please feel free to email: rainbow@shaftesburyschool.co.uk. This will go directly to Mr Cooper and Miss Karai.

At Shaftesbury School we use the definition for SEN and for disability from the SEND Code of Practice (2014) and the Equality Act (2010). This states that:
SEN
A child or young person has special educational needs if he or she has a learning difficulty or disability which calls for special educational provision to be made for him or her. A learning difficulty or disability is a significantly greater difficulty in learning than the majority of others of the same age. Special educational provision means educational or training provision that is additional to, or different from, which is made generally for others of the same age in a mainstream setting in England.
Disability
Many children and young people who have SEN may have a disability under the Equality Act 2010 –that is ‘…a physical or mental impairment which has a long-term and substantial adverse effect on their ability to carry out normal day-to-day as asthma, diabetes, epilepsy, and cancer.
At Shaftesbury School it is our aim to identify any pupil who has a special educational need and/or disabilities as soon as possible. Indicators could include:
Pupil observation indicates that they may have additional needs in one (or more) of the four areas:
Concerns raised by parents/carers
Changes in behaviour
Liaison with external agencies
Health diagnosis by a paediatrician
Communication and Interaction
Cognition and Learning
Social, Mental and Emotional Health
Sensory/Physical Need
What should I do if I need to raise concerns about my child?
In the first instance please arrange to come in to school to speak with your child’s form teacher, subject teacher or House/Year Progress Leader. This may then result in a referral to the school Inclusion Lead, Mr Tim Gillett.
It is important for us to ensure that all students reach their full potential; therefore, where a student is identified as having special educational needs and/or disabilities, we take action to remove barriers to learning and we aim to put effective special education provision in place.
Support will always include ‘Quality First Teaching’ and can also include:
Extra Literacy support
Numeracy support
Small group work
In class support
School Nurse
Emotional Literacy Support Assistant (ELSA)
1:1 interventions
Visual Impairment Team
Hearing Impairment Team
Child & Adolescent Mental Health Service (CAMHS)
Special Educational Needs Support Service (SENSS)
Educational Psychologist Service
Child & Young People’s Speech & Language Therapy Service (CYP SALT Service)
Local Authority’s Local Offer & More Information
As of September 2014 every Local Authority will be required to publish information about services that they expect to be available in their area for children and young people from birth to 25 who have special educational needs and/or disabilities (SEND) and also services outside of the area which they expect children and young people from their area will use. This will be known as the ‘Local Offer’.
The Local Offer will put all the information about education, health and care services, leisure activities and support groups in one place. It has two main purposes:
Please find below our policies and plans relating to SEND, together with a link to our Local Offer. Further policies are available on the Policies page of this website.
The Dorset Family Information Service web site has the Local Authorities Local Offer and also information for parents and carers on mediation and conflict resolution.
